transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-03-09
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Marcus (Redwood SE), Samir (Verdant), Elena (Verdant), Tom (Verdant), Nia (Verdant SRE)

Summary (auto): Quick recap at top: tonight's call is focused on the air-gapped install steps, artifact delivery options (sideload, portable HDD, signed manifest), offline license activation flow, and a debugging session for a driver/kernel mismatch Verdant hit in staging. Also touched on KV cache prefetch and batching to hit latency SLOs under constrained NIC/IO.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Samir (Verdant): Samir here, Elena, Tom and Nia with me. Thanks.
[00:12] Jordan (Redwood): Cool. So goal today is to walk through the offline provisioning path, licensing handoff, and the kernel/driver issues you saw. Priya will drive the runtime stuff. Marcus will cover artifact manifest and signing.
[00:25] Priya (Redwood SE): Hey team. I'll try to keep this pragmatic — real world steps and what to watch for, because on-prem air gap tends to trip over tiny things like minor driver versions or firewall rules.
[00:38] Elena (Verdant): Yeah, we had a failed boot of the runtime when we moved to 525 drivers, something with cgroup errors and module load flapping.
[00:45] Marcus (Redwood): Ok noted. We'll go through the specific kernel module versions we ship and the compatibility matrix.
[00:50] Tom (Verdant): Also licensing — we need an offline flow that security signs off on, no external callbacks.
[00:55] Jordan (Redwood): That's expected. Our offline activation is a two-file exchange: a signed manifest from us and an activation blob you generate on-prem and send back via secure channel. Marcus will show the template.

[01:10] Marcus (Redwood): Slide-free demo: artifact bundle contains model shards, runtime binary, kernel hooks, and a signed manifest.json. We'll sign with our key, you verify against the public cert shipped in the bundle. If you want HSM-based verification, you can import our cert into your vault.
[01:28] Samir (Verdant): Are manifests large? we plan to ship via encrypted HDD; do we need streaming?
[01:34] Marcus (Redwood): Manifests are small JSONs. The heavy bits are the model shards. HDD is fine. For checksum integrity we recommend sha256 per file and a top-level signed index.

[01:50] Priya (Redwood SE): On runtime: two common failures post-install are (1) GPU driver mismatch where the runtime expects a certain CUDA/driver combo, and (2) missing kernel module permissions for our nv-kernel shim. On older kernels the module loader path is different and you'll see a segmentation or cgroup error.
[02:10] Nia (Verdant SRE): That's what we saw, error said 'failed to initialize device: no compatible devices found' but the driver was installed.
[02:18] Priya (Redwood SE): Right, sometimes the driver is present but the userland/cuBLAS vs runtime binary ABI mismatch causes that. We have a small driver-check script that validates: nvidia-smi, nvcc versions, cuBLAS, libcudnn and kernel module gv. We'll share the script.
[02:35] Tom (Verdant - Security): From security perspective we need steps documented for verifying bundle integrity and the license activation without internet. Also audit log of who did the activation.
[02:45] Jordan (Redwood): We have an audit mode in the offline activator — it creates a signed activation record you can store in your SIEM. No callback required. We'll provide the sample logs.

[03:02] Samir (Verdant): On the KV cache: if you boot cold in an air-gapped environment, the first requests spike latency. We need to warm caches or prepopulate with typical prefixes. Thoughts?
[03:12] Priya (Redwood SE): Two options: bundle a warmup dataset that we run as part of provisioning (prefixes/embedding warmups), or use a local persistent KV snapshot we ship that you load into the engine at startup. The snapshot approach saves time but increases bundle size.
[03:30] Elena (Verdant): Size concern — our remote racks have limited IO during initial deploy windows. HDD shipping preferred.
[03:36] Marcus (Redwood): Ship snapshots on HDD and then at first boot we map the KV files into memory with mmap and do asynchronous prefetch of hot KV sets. That reduces blocking latencies.

[03:54] Priya (Redwood SE): For batching and quantization: in an on-prem environment if you can tolerate slightly higher tail latency you get huge unit-cost savings with 4-bit quant on supported models. But with air-gapped low IO, the KV prefetch becomes more important to avoid stutter for batched requests.
[04:14] Samir (Verdant): Are there recommend batch sizes for 8-bit vs 4-bit? We saw tokenization CPU spikes for large batches.
[04:22] Priya (Redwood SE): We typically start with target latency SLO and back-calc batch size. Example: for <200ms 95th you might use batch of 6-8 on A100 40GB with io-limited backplane; for throughput jobs where 500ms tail is fine, batches of 32-64 may be ok. We'll provide a perf matrix.

[04:45] Marcus (Redwood): Also watch the quantization profile: activation quant vs weight-only quant has different behavior for seq length. Our recommend profiles are in the quant-profile.yaml we'll attach.

[05:00] Tom (Verdant - Security): One question: how do you handle secret material (license keys) in the bundle if it's going to be on portable media?
[05:08] Jordan (Redwood): We don't put secret license keys in the bundle. The bundle contains our public cert and a template manifest. You generate an activation request from the machine, sign it with your org key, send that via a vetted channel, we return an encrypted activation blob that you can inject locally. The activation flow can be done completely offline with a USB shuttle if needed.

[05:30] Nia (Verdant SRE): Ok, practical: we tried to load the kernel module but modprobe failed—error code referencing unresolved symbol. What am I missing?
[05:38] Priya (Redwood SE): That usually means mismatch between compiled module version and kernel headers. Two ways: compile the shim against your exact kernel (we provide source + build script), or use our prebuilt module but ensure kernel ABI is supported. We maintain modules for common enterprise kernels (RHEL 8.6, Ubuntu 22.04, 5.15 family) but for custom kernels you must build locally.
[05:56] Samir (Verdant): We are on a patched 5.19 variant. Will need to build. Can you provide a deterministic build container?
[06:04] Marcus (Redwood): Yes we can provide a reproducible container image (OCI tarball) that contains the compiler, exact headers, and the module source, so you can build in air-gapped env. We'll include a GPG-signed container manifest.

[06:20] Priya (Redwood SE): Keep an eye on the rmmod order if you update drivers live, the runtime expects the module to expose certain ioctl paths. If the module unloads in wrong order you get hung processes.
[06:32] Nia (Verdant SRE): Good to know. We'll schedule maintenance window.

[06:40] Jordan (Redwood): Quick detour — networking: VPC-style private network in your datacenter. How is egress/firewall on the management plane?
[06:48] Tom (Verdant - Security): Management plane has outbound to our internal PKI and can't reach internet. That's why the offline activation requirement.
[06:54] Jordan (Redwood): That fits our offline model. Only requirement is ability to move files via controlled shuttle and a validated operator.

[07:05] Priya (Redwood SE): Back to perf: we recommend two phases for pilot: (1) functional smoke: install bundle, verify runtime starts, run driver-check, license activation; (2) perf week: run scripted workloads with warmup, measure p50/p95/p99 for both latency and throughput, and collect KV hit rates. We'll need sample prompts and a perf harness — we can provide that harness as an executable tarball.
[07:33] Elena (Verdant): Are there any telemetry callbacks baked into that harness? Our security team will need an allowlist.
[07:40] Jordan (Redwood): No callbacks. The harness is offline by default; it emits logs to local file and optionally to your syslog. We'll provide a pipeline for redaction if needed.

[07:52] Marcus (Redwood): On packaging: the bundle will have versions encoded: runtime_v, model_hash, driver_compat list, signed_manifest and the release_notes.md. The signed manifest is the authoritative piece for acceptance testing.
[08:06] Samir (Verdant): Good. For acceptance we need automated checks that verify the bundle and run the driver-test. Could you provide a Jenkinsfile or Ansible role?
[08:15] Marcus (Redwood): Yes, we have an Ansible role for artifact install and a CI/CD job example for offline activation. We'll drop both into the repo.

[08:28] Priya (Redwood SE): A few gotchas we've seen: (1) mismatch in libc version for the runtime binary on older distros leading to startup fails, (2) if you enable strict SELinux policies the runtime needs a policy module, (3) IO scheduler on some storage stacks can cause token emission stalls. We'll produce checklists for each.
[08:48] Tom (Verdant - Security): SELinux will be enforced for our images. We'll need the policy module + permissions documented.
[08:55] Priya (Redwood SE): We'll include the .te policy and example semodule build steps in the bundle.

[09:05] Jordan (Redwood): Let's step through the activation flow live — Marcus, can you narrate?
[09:09] Marcus (Redwood): Sure. Step 1: you run 'redwood-activator --generate-request --output req.bin' on the air-gapped host. Step 2: copy req.bin to a secure jump host, sign or wrap per your org policy, and forward to Redwood via secure channel (we accept SFTP over a customer-managed transfer or encrypted courier). Step 3: Redwood returns activation.blob which you load on host with 'redwood-activator --apply activation.blob' which writes a local license and writes an audit record.
[09:39] Samir (Verdant): For the signing step, can we substitute with our HSM-signed envelope?
[09:44] Marcus (Redwood): Yes, we support HSM-signed envelopes. We'll validate signature using the public key you provide or use our verification flow if you import our cert locally.

[09:56] Priya (Redwood SE): Time for a short troubleshooting demo. We reproduced a similar modprobe unresolved symbol issue locally. Watch the logs — there are subtle clues (symbols a,b,c missing).
[10:08] Priya (Redwood SE): [shares screen] see here: the kernel shows symbol 'nv_shim_alloc' unresolved which maps to our shim compiled against newer internal API. Means prebuilt module incompatible. Solution: build with your kernel headers or use our container.
[10:26] Nia (Verdant SRE): Ok that matches our logs. We'll opt to build locally. Please attach the container tar.

[10:33] Jordan (Redwood): We'll attach the signed container and the build instructions. Also include pins for gcc and glibc versions to be deterministic.

[10:42] Samir (Verdant): On quantization: if we do 4-bit, are there changes to the kernel module? Anything kernel-level?
[10:49] Priya (Redwood SE): No kernel-level changes. Quantization lives in the runtime userland and affects memory layout. But quant has different memory stride behaviors which can interact with our GPU allocator — so we recommend enabling our telemetry which logs allocator fragmentation statistics. It's writable locally, no outbound call.

[11:10] Elena (Verdant): For the perf week, we want to measure bursty traffic with mixed prompt lengths. Any recommended harness config?
[11:18] Priya (Redwood SE): Yes — we provide a config with 3 traffic profiles: 1) short-chat (avg 40 tokens), 2) long-generation (avg 400 tokens), 3) high-throughput embeddings. Run each for 2 hours with warmup phase 30 minutes. That will exercise KV warmup and batching.

[11:40] Tom (Verdant - Security): A question on logs: we need to ensure PII is not written. How do you handle redaction?
[11:47] Jordan (Redwood): The runtime has a redaction hook and you can configure a regex or a tokenization-based redactor. The perf harness has an option to enable scrubbers before writing logs. We'll provide default rules.

[12:02] Marcus (Redwood): Action item note: We'll include a driver-compat matrix CSV and a script 'driver-check.sh' in root of the bundle. Also the reproducible build container tarball (signed).
[12:12] Samir (Verdant): Great. On deployment windows we have strict change windows — can we do a dry-run that does everything except applying activation?
[12:20] Marcus (Redwood): Yes, 'redwood-activator --dry-run' exists and returns the same logs, checks, and would create the activation request file without changing state.

[12:30] Priya (Redwood SE): Quick note on telemetry: we collect only operational metrics if enabled, like token throughput, KV hit rates, and quant-induced allocator stats. No model prompts are sent anywhere by default. That aligns with your security ask.
[12:46] Tom (Verdant - Security): That's fine but we need to see the telemetry schema.
[12:50] Jordan (Redwood): We'll share schema and a sample logfile.

[13:00] Nia (Verdant SRE): Another gotcha — during our first test the runtime hit OOM when we loaded multiple model variants. Any tuning knobs?
[13:08] Priya (Redwood SE): Yes, use pinned cold-start pools with controlled parallelism and limit prefetch threads. Also enable our on-disk kv swap for low-memory machines. We'll add recommended values.

[13:26] Samir (Verdant): Competitive question: we evaluated triton and in-house earlier. Why Redwood runtime vs Triton for our workload?
[13:35] Jordan (Redwood): Two differentiators: (1) our unified model catalog with tested quant profiles and fast fallbacks between variants, and (2) production routing and built-in KV prefetching tuned for LLM workloads — Triton is strong but often requires more glue. We can run a side-by-side if you want.
[13:52] Elena (Verdant): Side-by-side would be useful.

[14:00] Marcus (Redwood): Ok, let's recap next steps and owners before we wrap.
[14:05] Jordan (Redwood): Recap: Redwood to send signed container tar, driver-check script, offline activator runbook, Ansible role, quant-profile.yaml, telemetry schema, and signed manifest template by 2026-03-11.
[14:20] Priya (Redwood SE): Verdant to run driver-check.sh, attempt local module build with the tar, and upload logs to the secure bucket by 2026-03-13.
[14:30] Samir (Verdant): We'll aim for the perf pilot week starting 2026-03-22 and will coordinate a maintenance window.
[14:36] Tom (Verdant - Security): We'll review the runbook and respond with any redaction or policy questions by 2026-03-12.
[14:42] Jordan (Redwood): Perfect. Any other questions?
[14:45] Elena (Verdant): Not at the moment. This was helpful.
[14:48] Jordan (Redwood): Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with the artifacts and a calendar invite for the pilot kickoff.
[14:55] Samir (Verdant): Thanks all.

End of transcript.
